newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu opponents shut down Kinshasa for second day.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu opponents shut down Kinshasa for second day.

text.p: Opponents of President Mobutu Sese Seko effectively closed down Zaire's capital Kinshasa for a second successive day on Tuesday as part of their campaign to oust the veteran strongman.

Paramilitary security forces blocked off access roads to the city's volatile campuses, where anti-Mobutu students skipped classes at the request of the main opposition which also called for a drive-by protest to follow Monday's stay-at-home protest.

On the diplomatic front, Laurent Kabila's rebels, who now control half of the huge Central African nation including its mineral-rich economic heart, faced growing pressure to return to the negotiating table.
South Africa's deputy foreign minister told a parliamentary committee in Cape Town that Zaire could be on the brink of formal negotiations about a transition to democracy.

"What has happened in an interesting way in the last few days is that both parties have signalled their commitment to meet directly at the principal level in order to negotiate the future dispensation in Zaire," Aziz Pahad said.
In Kinshasa, gendarmerie units directed traffic on the central November 24 Avenue, on which are located two flashpoint campuses, notably the higher institute of commerce.
"We are not letting traffic through. Very soon the students will start snatching cars for their protest," one officer said.
Most shops and businesses in the city of five million people stayed shut. Residents, many fearing unrest, stayed home.

Witnesses said most troops had concentrated at the Gaba roundabout leading to the main University of Kinshasa campus but taxi drivers from the outlying suburbs reported seeing groups of students heading for an unknown destination.
Supporters of ousted prime minister Etienne Tshisekedi, Mobutu's arch political rival, have resorted to protests while Kabila's rebels pursue an armed campaign from the east of Zaire.
Tshisekedi supporters shut down the teeming capital with a widely observed stay-at-home order on Monday.

Pro-Tshisekedi protest organisers asked students to skip school and college on Tuesday and to turn out in vehicles. In the past, such protests have led to turmoil as students commandeered any vehicles on the street.
Mobutu, 66, declared a state of emergency last week and named an army prime minister, General Likulia Bolongo, shunting aside Tshisekedi after less than a week in the job.
Monday's protest sparked no serious incidents but Mobutu's new information minister, Kin-Kiey Mulumba, said on Monday that troops would act to keep order.
"Force must be at the service of the law," he told a news briefing after a cabinet meeting devoted to the growing crisis.
Pahad said Kabila, currently in Zaire's southern second city of Lubumbashi, was expected to visit South Africa shortly but he had no details on timing.
In Lubumbashi Kabila remained in seclusion, a day after arriving to mark the capture of Zaire's second city.

Lubumbashi's one million people were still awaiting a rally, a victory parade or even a clear glimpse of Kabila, who swept into town on Monday in Mercedes jeep with dark-tinted windows, in the middle of a convoy of soldiers.
Washington has joined calls for Kabila to negotiate.

"If there's a way to resolve the civil war peacefully through negotiations in South Africa, we think that's far better than having the rebels advance on Kinshasa," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Monday.
U.S., French, Belgian and British troops are in neighbouring Congo to evacuate their nationals from Kinshasa if need be.
